paras: The lynching of John Diggs took place shortly before dawn on 27 July 1880, when about fifty men forced the jail at Rockville, Maryland, took Diggs, a Black man, from the sheriff and hanged him on the road toward Darnestown. Diggs had been arrested the night before, accused of assaulting Mrs. James Tschiffely, a white woman, near Darnestown. The story ran in short wire briefs across the country, and Democratic and other white editors cited it in arguments over Southern violence.

According to a Baltimore dispatch of 26 July, a man named in the report as John Biggs entered the Tschiffely home near Darnestown, in Montgomery County, while her husband was away on business. The dispatch said he choked her, held her in her room overnight, assaulted her repeatedly and struck her with a chair before escaping. The case caused 'the widest excitement' locally, and bands of men organized to search for him.
Diggs was captured at or near Mechanicsville on the night of 26 July, by a T. J. Davis according to one dispatch, and lodged in the Rockville jail.

Shortly before 4 a.m. the next morning, about fifty men appeared at the jail, and one of them asked to be let in on the plea of identifying the prisoner. Sheriff Kelchner refused while the crowd remained, and when a deputy hesitated at a second demand, the men broke in the door. A melee with the officers followed, and when the sheriff tried again to rescue his prisoner outside, two or three men held him and he was cut on the arm.

The crowd hurried Diggs, still in ankle irons, up the road toward Darnestown, where confederates had brought a horse. According to the long Washington wire, Diggs acknowledged the crime but refused to give details, and his calm 'awakened suspicion even among the party'. Finding it impracticable to hang him from the horse, the men put a noose over a tree limb and lifted his body from the ground. The crowd then dispersed quietly and left the body hanging.

Later that morning Sheriff Kelchner stated that Diggs had made a full confession to him before the jail was forced, a claim that rests on his word alone. No report of an inquest, of arrests among the crowd or of any official inquiry appears in the coverage. On 6 August the Montgomery County Sentinel's Darnestown correspondent reported that Mrs. Tschiffely was improving and might keep the eye 'so badly injured by the fiend Diggs', and blamed intemperance for the crime in a plea for local option.

The fullest account was a Washington wire printed as 'Lynch Law in Maryland', which the Juniata Sentinel ran with the subhead 'Hanging of a Negro for an Atrocious Assault Upon a White Woman'. That wire called Diggs 'the brute' and 'the villain' and his hanging an 'execution', yet it also described the crowd as men who had taken 'the law in their own hands'. Between 1 and 7 August most papers, among them the Milan Exchange, the Mower County Transcript, the Mankato Free Press and the Iola Register, carried only a sentence or two in news summaries.

Their wording varied: the Redwood Gazette called the lynchers 'a band of indignant citizens', the Connecticut Western News 'masked men', and the Elko Independent called Diggs 'another negro ravisher'. The Butler Citizen remarked that 'Lynching negroes for assaults upon women is becoming very common in the south', naming Rockville as the latest case.

Editors also turned the case to partisan use: the Democratic Columbian of Bloomsburg, Pennsylvania, cited it among 'outrages committed by Southern negroes upon white people' to argue that Republicans exaggerated Southern violence. The Sedalia Bazoo of Missouri mocked a prayer said to have been offered by a newspaperman at the hanging of 'the Maryland negro ruffian'.

Most reports, including both Washington dispatches, placed the hanging just before 4 a.m. on Tuesday, 27 July, while the Connecticut Western News said 'Monday night' and the Redwood Gazette 'about ten o'clock' that morning. The victim's name appeared as Diggs in most papers and in the local Sentinel, but as 'Biggs' in one dispatch and 'Drogs' in another.

reader.title: Lynching of John Diggs
bases: About fifty men forced the Rockville jail, took John Diggs, a Black man accused of assaulting a white woman, from the sheriff's custody and hanged him outside town (A2, A3, A8, A9).

Diggs was hanged by a crowd of about fifty men (40 or 50 in one dispatch) who broke into the jail against the sheriff's resistance, with no lawful authority, as punishment for an alleged assault on a white woman (A2, A3, A9, A13).

Two separate wire dispatches (the long Washington account in A2/A3 and the shorter Washington, July 27 report in A9) and several independent briefs (A5, A6, A7, A8) agree that a mob took Diggs from the Rockville jail and hanged him, and the local Montgomery County sentinel refers to the alleged crime of 'Diggs' (A14).

accounts.label: Washington wire (long version)
accounts.gist: About fifty men forced the jail before 4 a.m. despite the sheriff, took Diggs up the Darnestown road where a horse had been prearranged, and lifted him by a noose; Diggs acknowledged the crime but would not give details, and the sheriff said he had confessed fully.

accounts.label: Washington, July 27 dispatch (short version)
accounts.gist: 'John Biggs', captured by T. J. Davis, was taken by 40 or 50 men who surrounded the jail and broke the door after being refused, and was hanged from a tree limb; the crowd quietly dispersed.

accounts.label: Sheriff's statement
accounts.gist: Sheriff Kelchner said Diggs made a full confession to him before the jail was forced; this is the officer's claim, reported without other confirmation.

accounts.label: Local Darnestown correspondent
accounts.gist: The Rockville paper's Darnestown items treated Diggs's guilt as settled ('the fiend Diggs') and reported Mrs. Tschiffely's recovery, without describing the lynching.

framing.detail: The long wire, headed 'Lynch Law in Maryland' with the subhead 'Hanging of a Negro for an Atrocious Assault Upon a White Woman', called Diggs 'the brute' and 'the villain' and the hanging his 'execution', while noting that his calm 'awakened suspicion even among the party who thus took the law in their own hands'.
Short briefs in Tennessee, Minnesota, Missouri, Kansas, Indiana and Wisconsin papers stated the hanging in one or two sentences, some calling the mob 'indignant citizens'.
The Democratic Columbian cited the lynching as one of the 'outrages committed by Southern negroes upon white people' to turn the 'bloody shirt' against Republicans.
The Sedalia Bazoo mocked the 'irreverence' of a prayer said to have been offered by a newspaperman, while calling Diggs 'the Maryland negro ruffian'.
The local Montgomery County sentinel called Diggs 'the fiend' and discussed only the woman's recovery and intemperance as the cause of the crime.

conflicts.note: Most reports, including both Washington dispatches, put the hanging just before 4 a.m. on 27 July; 'Monday night' describes the same hours loosely, while the 10 a.m. time in A7 stands alone. The A2 dateline 'July 20' is a misprint: the identical wire in A3 is dated 'July 27'.
Diggs is the spelling in most reports and in the local Rockville paper; the others appear to be typesetting variants of one name.
